analysis.one_liner: Guarantees employees of large employers twelve weeks of unpaid leave for a new child or a serious illness.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in January 1993, referred to three House committees, and never received a vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would give employees who have worked at least a year for a large employer the right to take up to 12 weeks of unpaid leave for the birth or adoption of a child, to care for a seriously ill family member, or to deal with their own serious health problem, with the right to return to the same or an equivalent job and to keep their health insurance during the leave. It applies to employers with 100 or more employees, and extends the same rights to federal workers and congressional staff. The leave would be unpaid, and employers could deny job restoration to their highest-paid 10 percent of workers in some cases. It was introduced a week before a broader version of the same leave guarantee became law through a different bill, and this version never came up for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Employees of employers with 100 or more workers who need time off for a birth, adoption, foster placement, or a serious health condition of their own or a family member, plus federal civil servants and congressional employees.

how_it_helps.text: Entitles employees with 12 months of service and 1,500 hours in the prior year to 12 workweeks of unpaid leave for a birth or adoption, care of a spouse, child, or parent with a serious health condition, or their own serious health condition.
Requires the employer to restore the worker to the same or an equivalent position on return and to maintain group health coverage during the leave.
Makes it unlawful for an employer to interfere with or retaliate against workers exercising these rights, and lets workers sue for lost wages, reinstatement, and attorney's fees.
Extends the same leave rights to federal civil service employees and to Senate and House employees.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 100 or more employees, who would hold jobs open for up to 12 weeks, keep paying the employee's health premiums during unpaid leave, and face lawsuits for damages if they violate the law. Costs could be passed to customers in small part.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large employers bearing leave and compliance costs

drawbacks.text: The leave is unpaid, so workers who cannot afford to go weeks without a paycheck would get protection on paper but little practical help.
It covers only worksites with at least 100 employees (counting an employer's workers within 75 miles), leaving workers at small and mid-sized firms with no federal guarantee.

Employers could deny job restoration to the highest-paid 10 percent of workers within 75 miles of a facility, and spouses working for the same employer could be limited to a shared 12 weeks for birth, adoption, or parental-care leave.
Employers bear real costs: holding positions open, maintaining health premiums during unpaid leave, recordkeeping, and damages liability in court actions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is genuine job security at a moment when many workers previously had none, and the bill is built with guardrails: notice requirements, medical certification, employer second opinions, and a 100-employee threshold that keeps the smallest firms out. Its biggest weakness is that unpaid leave is only usable by workers who can absorb lost pay, so the benefit skews toward households with savings or a second income. The costs to covered employers are modest relative to a national labor force guarantee, though not zero.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees and then to subcommittees, and it sat there until the Congress ended in January 1995 without ever being reported out or voted on.

narrative.text: Representative Amo Houghton, a New York Republican, introduced the bill on January 27, 1993, with no cosponsors.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committees on Education and Labor, Post Office and Civil Service, and House Administration.
In February 1993 it was further referred to subcommittees; no markup, report, or vote appears in the record for the rest of the Congress.
The bill would have guaranteed 12 weeks of unpaid family and medical leave to employees of employers with 100 or more workers, with job restoration, continued health coverage, and court enforcement.
The 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 with the bill still in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers lost little, because Congress enacted a broader version of the same guarantee — the Family and Medical Leave Act of 1993, covering employers with as few as 50 employees — which the President signed on February 5, 1993, days after this bill was introduced. This narrower duplicate was effectively unnecessary, and no group's interests turned on its death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one — a broader law passed anyway

for.name: Rep. Amo Houghton
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Family and Medical Leave Act of 1993 in the House on January 27, 1993.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never reported it back for a House vote.

against.name: Rep. William Ford
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee that received the bill; the bill was never scheduled for markup or floor action.

against.name: House Committee on Post Office and Civil Service
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and passed it to a subcommittee; no further action was taken.

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral; no action followed.

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew no recorded votes and no cosponsors, so no partisan split shows in its record; its only sponsor was a Republican, while the broader family-leave law enacted that same session passed with bipartisan support in both chambers.

industries.note: The bill would require them to hold jobs open for up to 12 weeks of unpaid leave, maintain health premiums during leave, and face damages lawsuits for violations. The compliance cost is the flip side of the job security ordinary workers would gain.

industries.industry: Small and mid-size employers (under 100 employees within 75 miles)
industries.note: They would be exempt from the leave mandate entirely, which spared them costs but also meant their employees would receive no federal leave guarantee.
